newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Tight Yugo policy may cause recession - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Tight Yugo policy may cause recession - analysts.

text.p: Yugoslavia's government and central bank have signalled the economy is heading for a year of zero growth in retail prices which independent economists said on Tuesday would be coupled with recession.
"Zero inflation can be achieved only if absolutely restrictive monetary policy is applied," Stojan Stamenkovic of the Institute of Economic Sciences said.
Stamenkovic cautioned that sticking to restrictive money policy would halt all economic activity.
"A tighter monetary policy would mean no fresh commercial bank lending, a new recession in industry, a plunge in the standard of living and growing unemployment," he said.
National Bank of Yugoslavia (NBY) Vice-Governor Ratko Banovic said on Tuesday that in December 1997 there would be zero growth in retail prices compared to December 1996.
According to some estimates, the average 1997 inflation rate carried over from 1996 would stand at around 17.4 percent. In 1996, the carried-over inflation was close to 44 percent.
Economists agree that at the end of 1996 inflation as measured by the retail price index would be close to 60 percent.
Banovic also said the NBY would resort to even tighter money policy in 1997 to ensure overall economic stability and keep the dinar fixed at 3.3 to the German mark.
But Stamenkovic insisted that the zero price increase in 1997 was only an assumption. "The question is whether the government can control the zero inflation."
A more restrictive monetary stance implied money supply growth only by the volume of hard currency inflow, he said.

Zoran Popov of the Economics Institute said a zero or a 30 percent inflation did not make much difference for the Yugoslav economy. "A monthly inflation of up to 2 percent would be a fantastic success for our economic policy."
Some prices in Yugoslavia were far above the world levels and it was desirable for producers to reduce them, he said.
"But the impulse should come from the government itself. The government must reduce taxes and other fiscal contributions to allow companies to get rid of surplus workers," he added.
According to some estimates, Yugoslavia's state sector has 600,000 to 800,000 surplus workers apart from 26.5 percent of the officially unemployed.
If all surplus workers were laid off, the country would have around 1.5 million people employed, and the same number of unemployed and pensioners, economists said.
Popov insisted the government had to allow companies to perform under similar conditions as foreign competitors.
Ratko Banovic of the NBY cautioned that producers have piled up stocks over past three months, keeping prices high.
"You should start selling these stocks off and you can sell only if you cut prices," Banovic told businessmen on Tuesday.

Popov insisted the key issue remained whether the state could reduce public spending in a way that was economically, politically and socially acceptable. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
